idiom_name: request id field on the wire + correlation table (id -> waiter) on the requestor
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: mint a request id before publishing, put it in a reserved header or property of the request together with the reply address, register the waiter under that id in a table, then publish. The reader/dispatch side looks the id up, removes the entry and hands the payload to the waiting caller. The requestor owns the whole structure; the replier only copies the request id into the reply's correlation field and needs no knowledge of who is waiting. Pair every entry with a deadline, drop ids that do not resolve instead of failing, and keep the id reserved long enough that a late reply cannot satisfy a later request. Where the runtime provides one-shot awaitables (future, promise, continuation, channel), use them as the pending entry directly. For OpenTelemetry, use the W3C Trace Context propagators (traceparent/tracestate) to carry the id across HTTP and messaging hops automatically.
code_sketch:
id = new_id()
pending[id] = waiter(deadline)          # register BEFORE publishing
publish(request{ header.id: id, reply_to: my_reply_address, body })
reply = waiter.await()                  # deadline -> remove entry, report no-reply
# reader loop:
#   waiter = pending.remove(reply.header.correlation_id)
#   waiter ? waiter.deliver(reply.body) : log_and_drop(reply)
pitfalls: Registering the entry after the send: a fast reply can win the race and be dropped as unknown.
An id that is only unique per connection, or is reused after a restart, so a late reply satisfies a new request.
No deadline on the entry: replies that never come accumulate in the table forever.
Letting the replier hold requestor state (a session, a lock, a per-request channel) instead of copying one field.
Placing the id only inside the payload instead of in transport-level headers or message metadata, so intermediaries cannot see or forward it.
Using the same id for the entire conversation instead of per-message: loses the ability to correlate individual round-trips in a multi-leg operation.
Trusting the correlation field from an untrusted peer without validating its format — enabling log injection or cross-subsystem id collisions.

Wrong move: reusing the MessageId as the request id -> an intermediary (Message Router, smart proxy) creates a new message with its own MessageId, so the echoed correlation matches no pending entry and every reply through that hop times out -> instead generate a conversation-scoped id independently at the originator and have every participant copy it unchanged.

Wrong move: using the correlation id as a deduplication or idempotency key -> retries, replays and saga steps legitimately carry the same id, so valid messages get discarded as duplicates -> instead key deduplication on a per-message idempotency key and treat the correlation id only as a grouping label.

Wrong move: expecting correlation-id log search alone to explain a slow or broken flow -> ids group evidence but carry no timing or causal structure, and overlapping retries make a shared id ambiguous -> instead pair the correlation id with traces and metrics, and use trace/span or causation links for the hierarchy.
